How many people can ask EdgeQuake at once?

We pointed a load generator at the shared demo and kept adding people until answers got too slow. Everything below is measured, on one named Google Cloud server, and explained in plain English.

The short answer. For a short burst the demo handled up to 12 people asking fresh questions at once (it first missed at 14). Kept up for 3.5 minutes on end, it sustained a non-stop crowd of 8 and a steady stream of 30 questions a minute. The VM was the bottleneck: its CPU sat at 90% or more for 32% of the measured time (peak 100%), and the “look up” step running on the VM grew from 1.2 s to 20.0 s per answer as the crowd grew, while the external LLM steps barely moved (7.3 s → 7.9 s).

“On time” always means: answered successfully within 25 seconds. A level passes when at least 90% of its answers are on time.

1. The question, in plain English

A demo can feel fast when one person uses it and slow when a whole team does. We wanted to know where that change happens: how many people can ask brand-new questions at the same moment and still get an answer in about 25 seconds, most of the time (at least 9 answers in 10).

The point where it stops meeting that promise is called the knee. Below the knee, adding people costs little. Past it, everyone waits longer and fewer good answers come out per second.

2. The server that was tested

The public demo at demo.edgequake.com is not a serverless service and not a large cluster. It is one small Google Cloud virtual machine running four containers. The exact facts below were read from Google Cloud and from the VM itself at the start of the run.

3. How the test works — in plain English

Think of the demo as a coffee counter. One barista (the server) takes an order, phones a specialist supplier (the LLM), and hands the drink over. We want to know how big the queue can get before customers wait too long.

The recipe

  1. Check the counter is open. We read /health and /ready and send one real, authenticated question. If the server is unhealthy or rejects our key, the run stops (BLOCKED) instead of measuring garbage.
  2. Use real, never-repeated questions. Questions are about the papers already uploaded to the demo workspace. Every “fresh” question carries a one-off tag, so the server cannot reuse a stored answer. This measures real work, not memory.
  3. Turn the dial two different ways (Figure 3): H1 — a fixed crowd of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 20 people each asking again as soon as they get an answer; H2 — new questions arriving at a steady rate of 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 per second, whether or not earlier ones have finished.
  4. Score every answer. An answer is good only if it came back successfully, was not empty, and took under 25 seconds (and, for fresh questions, was not a cache hit). A load level passes if at least 90% of its answers are good, fewer than 5% errors occur and fewer than 3 “too many requests” replies are seen.
  5. Find the knee. The knee is the last level that passes before the first one that fails. Because you asked us to push further, we kept going past the knee to watch how the service degrades, with safety brakes: stop if over 25% of requests error, 10 or more “too many requests” replies appear, or under 10% of answers are good.
  6. Test the easy case separately (H3). The same three FAQ questions are asked over and over by up to 32 people. Those are answered from a cache, so they are reported on their own and never mixed into the fresh-question capacity.
  7. Check it holds up (H4). We hold the comfortable crowd steady for several minutes to see whether answers slowly get slower. This turned out to matter: a small shared-core VM is allowed to run flat-out only for about two minutes (see “burst vs sustained” below).
  8. Find the sustained ceiling (H5). We rest the server for a few minutes so its burst allowance refills, apply one steady load for 3½ minutes, and judge only the part after the first two minutes. A load that still passes there is something the server can do all day.
  9. Watch the server while it happens. Every few seconds we read the VM’s CPU, memory and per-container usage (read-only) to see whether the hardware or the LLM was the limit.
Rules of fair play
  • One tenant and one workspace (IDs in the header), same model throughout.
  • Fresh questions never repeat; FAQ tests are reported separately.
  • Never more than 32 people at once, and never faster than 0.6 questions/s.
  • Every request and its timings are saved (units.jsonl).
What we did not do
  • No document uploads, deletes or OCR on the shared demo.
  • We do not judge answer quality (that is a different benchmark).
  • We do not claim this is “the” capacity of EdgeQuake — only of this VM and this LLM account, on this day.

4. Result 1 — a crowd of people asking fresh questions (H1)

In one sentence. Up to 12 people asking at the same instant, at least 90% of fresh questions were answered within 25 seconds (typical wait 17.1 s, slowest-tenth starting at 22.9 s). The first level to miss was 14. Good answers per second peaked at 0.52/s with 12 people at once. Beyond that, more people mostly added waiting rather than more answers. At the burst limit an answer spends about 8.0 s in the external-LLM steps and 6.8 s in the lookup on our own VM (Figure 7).

5. Result 2 — questions arriving on their own schedule (H2)

In one sentence. For a 90-second window the demo kept up with a steady stream of about 36 fresh questions per minute (0.6/s); even our top rate of 0.6/s (36/min) did not break it, so the true limit is higher than we tested for that short window (the sustained test below shows the longer-term limit).

In real life nobody waits politely for the person before them. Here new questions arrive at a fixed rate for 90 seconds per level. If the server is slower than the arrivals, the backlog grows and every later answer is later still.

What that means for people online (illustration, not a measurement)

People spend most of their time reading and thinking, not waiting. By Little’s law, people online ≈ arrival rate × (thinking time + wait). With the sustained rate of 0.5 questions/s (30/min) and a typical 8.9 s wait:

Behaviour (assumed)Time between asksPeople online the demo could carry
Very active (asks a question every ~30 s)30s≈ 19 people
Typical (a question every ~2 min)120s≈ 64 people
Casual (a question every ~5 min)300s≈ 154 people

6. Result 3 — the same questions again and again (H3)

In one sentence. When 32 people asked the same three FAQs, 100% were served from the answer cache with a typical wait of 18.5 s, versus 8.5 s for a fresh question on a quiet server.

Note: even cache hits show multi-second waits at high concurrency. That is queueing in front of the small VM, not LLM time, which is why the FAQ figures are reported separately and never counted as fresh-question capacity.

7. Result 4 — does it hold up over time? (H4 soak)

In one sentence. Holding 12 people asking non-stop for 4 minutes produced 95 answers, 24% on time. Typical wait moved from 26.1 s (first third) to 35.0 s (last third), a drift of +34% — so the crowd size that looked fine for two minutes could not be held.

This is the most important surprise of the test. The short sweeps above are honest, but they are short. When the same crowd stays for several minutes, the server slows down — the explanation is in the next section.

8. Result 5 — what the server can sustain (H5)

In one sentence. A non-stop crowd of 8 people and a steady stream of 30 questions a minute held up once the burst allowance was used up (3.5 minutes per level, judged after the first 2 minutes).

Burst vs sustained — the idea in plain English

The tested machine is a shared-core Google Cloud type (e2-medium). Google’s documentation says these machines are guaranteed only one vCPU’s worth of CPU time in total, and may borrow up to two full vCPUs for roughly two minutes when they have saved up credit while idle. Think of a phone plan with a fast-data allowance: everything is quick until the allowance runs out, then you are throttled.

So a load that looks fine in a two-minute sweep can be impossible to keep up. To measure the real, all-day capacity we (1) let the server rest for 150.0 s so the allowance refills, (2) apply one steady load for 210.0 s, and (3) ignore the first 120 s — the burst — and judge only what happens afterwards.

9. What the server was doing meanwhile

Verdict. The VM was the bottleneck: its CPU sat at 90% or more for 32% of the measured time (peak 100%), and the “look up” step running on the VM grew from 1.2 s to 20.0 s per answer as the crowd grew, while the external LLM steps barely moved (7.3 s → 7.9 s).

Peaks during the sweep — VM CPU 100% (95th percentile 100%), steal 0%, API container 93% / 226 MB, Postgres 415% / 366 MB; 411 samples. Container percentages come from Docker and are relative to one vCPU, so on this two-vCPU machine a single container can read above 100% (and, on a shared core, occasionally above 200%). Treat the top panel (whole-VM CPU) as the reliable saturation signal.

10. What you can and cannot say

Safe to say
  • “On the shared demo (e2-medium), for a short burst up to 12 people asking fresh questions at once got 9-in-10 answers within 25 s.”
  • “Sustained for several minutes, it held 8 people asking non-stop and about 30 fresh questions a minute.”
  • “Repeated FAQ questions are served from the cache almost regardless of the crowd.”
Do not say
  • “EdgeQuake supports N users” without naming the server, LLM, workspace, duration and date.
  • That the burst number is the everyday capacity — on this shared-core VM it is not.
  • That answer quality was tested — it was not.
  • That production hardware would behave the same.

What would raise the ceiling

  • Give the server more CPU. Move from the shared-core e2-medium to a dedicated-core type (for example e2-standard-4 or a compute-optimised type). Dedicated cores have no burst allowance to run out of.
  • Separate the database. Postgres (which holds the vectors and the knowledge graph) and the API compete for the same two vCPUs; give Postgres its own machine or a managed service.
  • Make the lookup cheaper. The “look up” step is the one that grows with the crowd — examine its queries (graph hops, number of vectors compared) before buying hardware.
  • Re-run this exact protocol afterwards and compare the sustained ceiling (Figure 13) with today’s.
  • Keep the answer cache on and warm it for common questions (FAQ answers cost almost nothing).

Glossary

Burst vs sustained
Burst: what a shared-core VM can do for its first ~2 minutes using saved-up CPU credit. Sustained: what it can do indefinitely.
Knee
The last load level that still meets the promise; just past it, waiting time climbs fast.
On time / attainment
The share of answers that arrived successfully within 25 seconds.
Typical wait (median, p50)
Half of answers were faster than this, half slower.
Slowest 10% (p90)
Nine in ten answers were faster than this number.
Closed loop
A fixed crowd; each person asks again after receiving an answer.
Open loop
Questions arrive at a steady rate regardless of whether earlier ones are done.
Cache hit
The server reused a stored answer instead of asking the LLM again.
Goodput
Good answers delivered per second — throughput that actually counts.
CPU steal
Time the VM wanted to run but the shared physical core was busy with another tenant.
Token
A word-piece; LLM work and cost are measured in tokens.
